archetype.name: Fringe Contender (defense-first)
archetype.definition: A roughly average team by play-for-play efficiency. Its top-ten run defense and pass rush keep games close enough for a below-average offense to steal some, and a soft back half of the schedule could push it into the wild-card conversation.

report.headline: A real defensive turnaround, an offense still stuck near 18 points a game
report.take:
Start with how far this team has come. Last season the Jets ranked dead last in net EPA (-0.271) and 30th in EPA allowed. Five games into Aaron Glenn's second year, they are 15th in net EPA and 7th in defensive EPA, and they allow 19.2 points a game, 5th in the league. The 2-3 record is honest: wins over expected is essentially zero (-0.06), the point differential is -0.6 a game, and the efficiency says .500 team. This is not a lucky team or an unlucky one. It is a middling team whose defense is now good and whose offense is not.

The defense is built on stopping the run (-0.177 rush EPA allowed, 7th) and finishing at the quarterback. Their 17 sacks rank 3rd and their 9.1% sack rate ranks 2nd. The pass defense underneath is ordinary: 18th in pass EPA allowed, 22nd on short throws, 23rd in success rate allowed. The scoreboard looks better than the down-to-down work because of situational defense, 8th on third down and 6th in red-zone TD rate. That gap between allowing a lot of successful plays and allowing few points is the first thing to expect to tighten.

The offense is Geno Smith throwing to Garrett Wilson behind a line that cannot protect him. Wilson has 42 of the targets, double anyone else. The line has allowed 16 sacks at a 9.2% rate (30th), and the run game gets only 1.99 yards before contact (27th). Penalties are a self-inflicted tax at 9.4 a game (30th); 156 penalty yards in the 3-point loss to Green Bay is the clearest example. The passing trend is the worry. Passing EPA was 9.8, 4.3 and 10.9 in the first three games, then -4.9 at Chicago and -11.3 against Cleveland. That Cleveland win was rescued by an 8-sack defensive afternoon.

Where it heads: the defense is real and should keep them in most games, but the sack totals are running well ahead of a pressure rate that ranks 30th, and that will cool. The schedule is the friend here, with Miami twice, the Chargers' 32nd-ranked offense and Arizona still to come. A finish in the 7-8 win range is the most likely outcome. The offense would have to stop leaking sacks and flags to get beyond it.

strengths.title: Run defense that forces dropbacks
strengths.body: Opponents lose value running at the Jets (-0.177 EPA per rush, 7th), and offenses pass against them 4.1 points less often than normal in neutral spots. Missed tackles are low (7.1%, 9th), so this is tackling and gap integrity rather than game-script noise. The one leak is explosives: 10.2% of runs go big (23rd), which is how Chicago got to 232 rushing yards. The base efficiency should hold.

strengths.title: Finishing sacks at an elite rate
strengths.body: Seventeen sacks and the league's 2nd-best sack rate have produced drive-killing negative plays, including 8 against Cleveland. The rush converts nearly every pressure it gets, which is a skill but also a fragile one. The pressure rate itself is 30th, so expect the sack pace to slow even if the defense stays good.

strengths.title: Stingy where points are decided
strengths.body: Opponents convert just 33.9% on third down and score touchdowns on half their red-zone trips. That is why a defense allowing a 44.7% success rate still gives up only 19.2 points a game. Situational rates like these tend to drift toward the overall success rate, so this is the part of the profile most likely to slip.

concerns.title: Pass protection is sinking drives
concerns.body: Smith is taken down on 9.2% of dropbacks (30th), with 16 sacks in five games. Only 0 of those came in the opener. His time to throw is league-average (2.932, 15th), so this is not simply a quarterback holding the ball. The line is losing reps. With guard Dylan Parham out, it is hard to see this improving soon.

concerns.title: Passing game trending the wrong way
concerns.body: After three positive passing games, the last two produced -4.9 and -11.3 passing EPA, the latter with two turnovers. Wilson is carrying a thin target tree. With Adonai Mitchell and Breece Hall out and Kenyon Sadiq in concussion protocol, the supporting cast gets thinner before it gets better.

concerns.title: Penalties are a real flaw
concerns.body: At 9.4 penalties a game (30th), with 4 a game from the line alone, the Jets hand back field position constantly. In a 2-3 start where only one of three one-score games went their way, flags have been the difference. This is discipline, not luck, and it has shown up in every week but one.

trend.note: The defense has been steady every week except Chicago's rushing day. The offense went from three positive passing games to two deeply negative ones, and it was rescued in Week 5 by an 8-sack defensive outing rather than by moving the ball.

nextGame.headline: Big road dog in Foxborough, but New England's secondary is gutted
nextGame.body:
New England is the better team (9th in net EPA vs. 15th), but the matchup splits in interesting ways. The Patriots throw well (9th in pass EPA) and run poorly (23rd), which is exactly the shape the Jets' run defense wants: it pushes Drake Maye into a dropback game. Maye's 3.057-second time to throw is the 3rd-longest in the league, and the Jets' rush converts pressure into sacks better than almost anyone, even if it doesn't generate much pressure. On the other side, the Patriots' run defense ranks 30th in EPA, which gives Braelon Allen a real lane despite the Jets' poor blocking.

Availability is the story. New England is listed without both starting corners, Carlton Davis III and Christian Gonzalez (95% snaps each), plus depth corners Channing Canada and Karon Prunty, with Charles Woods questionable. A.J. Brown's return estimate falls after this game, and left tackle Will Campbell and back TreVeyon Henderson are questionable. The Jets are without Parham, Mitchell and Hall, with Sadiq and edge Joseph Ossai questionable. That funnels nearly everything through Wilson against a decimated secondary already 24th in deep-ball EPA allowed. The early forecast shows 12 mph wind with gusts near 19, worth a glance but not a reason to change the read this far out.

keyMatchups.title: Garrett Wilson vs. backup corners
keyMatchups.body: New England's pass defense ranks 5th in EPA, but that was built with Davis and Gonzalez on the field, and both are out. The Patriots were already vulnerable deep, and Wilson should see a target share well above his season norm with Mitchell out and Sadiq uncertain.

keyMatchups.title: Jets sack finish vs. Maye's patience
keyMatchups.body: Maye holds the ball longer than all but two quarterbacks. The Jets don't pressure often but finish nearly every pressure they get. If Campbell sits at left tackle, this is where the Jets can steal possessions.

keyMatchups.title: Allen against a soft run front
keyMatchups.body: The Patriots allow positive rushing EPA nearly every week (30th). The Jets' line gets backs just 1.99 yards before contact, and Parham is out. This matchup decides whether the Jets can stay on schedule rather than leaning on Smith behind a leaky line.

nextGame.watch: How many sacks the Jets give up on early downs. If Smith stays upright, the Patriots' missing corners make this a one-score game.

restOfSeason.body:
The defense is the foundation, and its core (run defense, tackling, a rush that finishes) should hold. Expect the points allowed to creep up toward 20-22 a game, for two reasons. The success rate allowed is middle-of-the-pack, and the third-down and red-zone numbers are outperforming it. The sack total will also slow, given a pressure rate near the bottom of the league. The +0.6 turnover margin is helped by a careful offense (3 giveaways in five games) and should drift toward even.

The offense probably stays in the 17-21 point range unless the protection and penalty problems get fixed. Neither has a quick fix with Parham out. The schedule is forgiving: two games with winless Miami, the Chargers' 32nd-ranked offense and Arizona. Two Buffalo games, Kansas City and an unbeaten Minnesota cap the ceiling. That points to 7-8 wins and fringe wild-card relevance rather than a real playoff push.
swingFactors: Health of Hall, Mitchell and Sadiq around Wilson
Whether the sack conversion survives a 30th-ranked pressure rate

bets.reason: The efficiency gap (0.063 vs 0.011 net EPA, point differential +3.2 vs -0.6) supports a home line closer to 4-5 than a hook past a touchdown. New England is also playing without both 95%-snap corners and has a -1.0 per-game turnover margin. The Jets are 3-1-1 against the spread on the back of a defense that has held four of five opponents to 23 or fewer.

Wilson already has double anyone else's targets. Mitchell (15 targets in two games) is out and Sadiq is in concussion protocol, so the volume concentrates further. It concentrates against a secondary missing Davis, Gonzalez and two depth corners that was already 24th in deep EPA allowed.

confidence.note: Five-game sample, heavy injuries on both sides, and a defensive profile partly built against weak offenses (TEN, CLE).
